title.narrative: Bananas in Pakistan's Bioeconomy: Transforming Waste into Textile

description.narrative: 1. A range of factors have historically promoted an overuse of chemicals, especially in Pakistan’s cotton production. These include vested business interests, harmful fiscal incentives, and subsidy schemes, alongside weak regulation and national tracking systems. Limited farmer education, gender inequalities, scarcity of expert advice and low analytical capacity in the field further exacerbate the problem. A lasting shift towards better and less consumption will have to tackle perceived and real trade-offs between sustainability and economic growth, in response to which the project aims to present a compelling business case for alternative raw materials, convening all key interest groups. The project will tackle the systemic challenges described in the barrier section by connecting the growing number of textile industries investing in bioeconomy innovations with farmers and producers of good quality, sustainable raw materials, which meet consumer demand[1]. The project activities like conducting socio-economic and global environmental benefits (health, employment, environment, etc.), techno-economic feasibility study of banana fibre extraction and softening and different products, will assess project interventions impacts on promoting better and green jobs in rural areas. In addition project activities like, developing sustainable banana production technologies and guidelines, implementing pilot scheme for traceability, developing Environmentally Sound Management (ESM) plan and Standards Operating Procedures (SOPs) will ensure improvement of labor standard and labour condition. The FAO 10 principles for a sustainable bioeconomy presented before could be used to ensure that no one is left behind in the development of the project. The project will develop a multistakeholder consultation process and involve different actors to be part of the design and reduce any tradeoffs between fibers. [1] Pakistan’s first Biennial Update Report to the UNFCCC (https://unfccc.int/documents/470405) and a 2022 Survey on the Agricultural Sector in Sindh Province (https://openjicareport.jica.go.jp/pdf/12368841.pdf demonstrate) emphasize persistent gender inequalities and related vulnerabilities in Pakistan at large, and Sindh in particular – while also making some recommendations that can inform project interventions. Notably, although Sindh is one of the first provinces in Pakistan to develop a legal framework for women's empowerment, many women in rural areas are involved in agricultural activities, women’s leadership of agricultural activities is limited in Sindh. Women’s empowerment varies greatly from village to village, and by community – for example, Muslim women are less likely to perform agricultural work than Hindu women. Context-appropriate engagement modalities and project activities will need to be shaped inclusively with project stakeholders during full project elaboration.

Accelerating bioeconomy transition in the Pakistan textile sector by transforming banana pseudo stem waste into economically viable and socially beneficial fibre and promoting Sustainable Agriculture Practices (SAP) in banana cultivation.
Note: Disbursement data provided is cumulative and covers disbursement made by the project Agency.
